Quotation guidance:

"""
# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.

5	## Brief
6	
7	Write a journalistic customer case for operations managers at small housing companies. The publisher is the supplier, Svale Systems. The customer, Elm Quay Housing, should remain the acting party. Approximately 400 words, as material allows. Markdown. No author name supplied. The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial.
8	
9	## Material
10	
11	Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings. Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately. The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information. It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.
12	
13	The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents. Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions. The trial lasted eight weeks. Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial. Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements.
14	
15	Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind, complete usable quotations:
16	
17	- “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”
18	- “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”
19	- “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”
20	
21	Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. It is not an inference from the figures. The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs. The supplier approved publication of this case as supplier-published material; it is not independent journalism. All interviews occurred by email, and no physical scene, emotion or remembered dialogue is provided. Translation of the quotations is permitted, preserving stance and qualification.
22	
23	## Forbidden inferences / judging
24

The customer's reservation must survive. Judge whether quotations contribute experience beyond the surrounding narrative, whether supplier narration stays in third person and whether the suggested link accurately describes its destination.

# Claim-support report 2: draft vs supplied material

Draft: scratch/write-run.uSsLSF/draft.md (English, en_US). Source: work/source.md (English). The source and draft are in the same language, so there is no translation of quotations. All three Lind quotations appear verbatim.

## A. Claim accounting

Each item gives the draft passage, the source passage in the source's own words, and what differs.

### Title
1. D: "Repair trial gives Elm Quay's team one view"
   S: "Having one view of the reports helps us" (Lind); "decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings"
   Differences: the title does not repeat the two-building scope, and "gives" is in the headline present tense. The standfirst supplies the scope immediately afterwards, and "one view" is Lind's own phrase. Headline present tense is a normal convention for a past event. **No finding** (see item 30 for the one place where the draft does claim a current state).

### Standfirst
2. D: "Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 apartments"
   S: "Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats."
   Differences: "apartments" is the en_US term for "flats". Nothing in this context falls under one term and not the other. **No finding.**
3. D: "tested a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two of its buildings"
   S: "its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings"; "The trial lasted eight weeks."; "It chose Svale Systems after testing…"
   Differences: the draft says "its buildings" where the source says "two buildings". Read in context, "its" means buildings under Elm Quay's management. Given "manages 640 flats", no case separates the two readings in any meaningful way. **No finding.**
4. D: "Its maintenance supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week for preparation"
   S: "I would choose to do the trial again. … but I would leave an extra week for preparation." Lind is "maintenance supervisor".
   Differences: "run" versus "choose to do". Both keep the conditional "would", and both mean conducting the trial again. "Its" is third person singular and neuter, and it refers to Elm Quay. It says nothing about Lind's gender. **No finding.**
5. D: "—a lesson for operations managers planning something similar"
   S: the brief names the audience as "operations managers at small housing companies".
   This is the author's framing, resting on Lind's supported statement. **No finding.**

### Opening
6. D: "telephone reports and emails used to be stored separately"
   S: "Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately."
   Matches. **No finding.**
7. D: "In September 2025 the company's own maintenance team decided to test a shared log in two buildings"
   S: "In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings."
   Differences: the draft calls Elm Quay a "company". The source never describes Elm Quay's organisational form. The brief's audience line ("operations managers at small housing companies") describes the readers, not Elm Quay. **Finding F2.**
8. D: "so that staff on different shifts could see the same information"
   S: "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information."
   The motive is supported and attributed to the team. **No finding.**
9. D: "After the eight-week trial, the team had a figure that Elm Quay's own trial note does not credit to the software"
   S: "The trial lasted eight weeks. Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025 … the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
   Differences: the draft says "figure" where the source says "difference". The note is dated after the trial. **No finding.**
10. D: "and a qualified verdict from its supervisor"
    S: "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment."
    Differences: "verdict" versus "assessment". The interview date is not given, but Lind's "do the trial again" presupposes that the trial is over, so "after" holds. "its" refers to the team, is neuter and carries no gender. **No finding.**

### Heading "Elm Quay tested repair tracking before picking Svale"
11. S: "It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair."
    Differences: "repair tracking" is a paraphrase of "whether the log could show the status of each repair", and the order of events is kept. **No finding.**

### Section 1
12. D: "In an email interview, maintenance supervisor Maya Lind puts the aim concretely: 'We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done.'"
    S: "All interviews occurred by email"; the quotation is verbatim.
    The quotation is the first sentence of quotation 1, and "the aim" matches "We wanted…". **No finding.**
13. D: "The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available."
    Verbatim. **No finding.**

### Heading "Elm Quay designed the categories, and Svale set up the system"
14. S: "The maintenance team designed its categories"; "Svale configured the log".
    Differences: "set up the system" versus "configured the log". Nothing is widened in a way the material would separate. **No finding.**

### Section 2
15. D: "Residents kept the option of reporting repairs by telephone; the team left that route open."
    S: "kept telephone reporting open for residents"
    Matches. **No finding.**
16. D: "Svale Systems configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions"
    S: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions."
    Matches. **No finding.**
17. D: "Lind is precise about the division of work: 'The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.'"
    The quotation is the second sentence of quotation 1, verbatim. "Precise" is the author's description of the quotation's content, not a factual claim. "us" and "ours" are Lind's own first person plural words, kept as spoken. **No finding.**
18. D: "Lind draws a practical lesson from the work: 'We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.'"
    Quotation 2 is verbatim. **No finding.**

### Heading "Median assignment time fell, but the note does not credit software"
19. S: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. … the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    Differences: "fell" describes a change between the two periods and is not causal. The heading carries the note's refusal to attribute the change. The source makes the same period-to-period comparison. **No finding.**

### Section 3
20. D: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
    Verbatim except for the en_US date format. "It" refers to the note and is neuter. **No finding.**
21. D: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, against three in the preceding eight-week period. The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
    Verbatim. **No finding.**
22. D: "Nor is assignment the same as completion. There are no measurements of completion time, cost, or resident satisfaction."
    S: "There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements." The brief says: "Do not turn assignment time into completion time."
    Matches. **No finding.**

### Heading "The supervisor would repeat the trial with more preparation"
23. S: "I would choose to do the trial again … I would leave an extra week for preparation."
    "More preparation" is a narrower rendering of "an extra week" that remains true. **No finding.**

### Section 4
24. D: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
    Verbatim. **No finding.**
25. D: "The assessment Lind does give is a qualified one, and it is not drawn from the figures"
    S: "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. It is not an inference from the figures."
    Matches. The source's "Her" conveys female natural gender, but the draft uses no gendered pronoun for Lind, so no gender is asserted. **No finding.**
26. D: quotation 3
    Verbatim. **No finding.**

### Heading "Expansion decision waits on how the categories handle larger repairs"
27. S: "the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs"
    Differences: "waits on" means "awaits", which is the same order of events as "decide after checking". **No finding.**

### Section 5
28. D: "The trial has not yet expanded."
    Verbatim. **No finding.**
29. D: "The team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs."
    S: "the categories". Earlier the source says "The maintenance team designed its categories", so "its" (the team's) is supported. **No finding.**
30. D: "That leaves Elm Quay with a shared view its supervisor says helps, a figure its note does not credit to the software, and a decision still ahead."
    S: "The trial lasted eight weeks."; "The trial has not yet expanded"; "Having one view of the reports helps us".
    Differences: the draft asserts that Elm Quay currently has the shared view. The source dates the trial as a closed eight-week period and never says whether the log stayed in use afterwards. **Finding F1.** The other two parts of the sentence are supported.

### Link
31. D: "For operations managers weighing a similar trial, [read the implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist)."
    S: "The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read".
    The link text describes the destination accurately. **No finding.**

### Byline
Excluded by instruction.

## B. Findings (source support)

**F1 (moderate, PLAUSIBLE): "That leaves Elm Quay with a shared view its supervisor says helps" (final paragraph before the link)**
- What is missing: support for the claim that Elm Quay still has the shared log or view now. The material says "The trial lasted eight weeks" and "The trial has not yet expanded". It is silent on whether the log stayed in use in the two buildings after the trial.
- Case where the draft fails: after the eight weeks the log was paused while the team checks the categories. Elm Quay then does not currently have a shared view, yet every supplied statement still holds. Lind's "Having one view of the reports helps us" is in the present tense, but it can be read generically and does not exclude this case.
- Smallest repair: "That leaves Elm Quay with a supervisor who says one view of the reports helps, a figure its note does not credit to the software, and a decision still ahead."

**F2 (minor, CONFIRMED as unsupported): "the company's own maintenance team" (opening paragraph)**
- What is missing: support for Elm Quay's organisational form. The material calls it "Elm Quay Housing" and "the customer". "Small housing companies" in the brief describes the target readers, not Elm Quay.
- Case where the draft fails: Elm Quay Housing is a housing association, cooperative or public body rather than a company. Nothing supplied excludes this.
- Smallest repair: "Elm Quay's own maintenance team" (or "the organisation's own maintenance team").

## C. Translation findings

None. Source and draft are both in English, and all quotations are verbatim.

## D. Completion status

Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, standfirst, headings, body and link was accounted for. The draft uses no gendered pronouns for Lind. Its pronouns ("its", "it") are neuter and refer to the organisation, team or note, and the first person pronouns inside quotations are Lind's own. Unresolved findings: F1 (present possession of the shared view) and F2 ("company"). Neither has been repaired in the draft, because this review does not change it.
